Main.sentence: Protestantism is a branch of ___E:Christianity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity)___ [a] that emphasizes ___E:justification U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justification_(theology))___ of sinners ___E:through faith alone U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sola_fide)___ , the teaching that ___E:salvation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvation_in_Christianity)___ comes by unmerited ___E:divine grace U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grace_in_Christianity)___ , the ___E:priesthood of all believers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priesthood_of_all_believers)___ , and the ___E:Bible U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bible)___ as the sole infallible source of authority for Christian faith and practice.
The ___E:five solae U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_solae)___ summarize the basic theological beliefs of mainstream Protestantism.

Protestants follow the ___E:theological U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_theology)___ tenets of the ___E:Protestant Reformation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformation)___ , a movement that began in the 16th century with the goal of reforming the ___E:Catholic Church U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church)___ from perceived ___E:errors, abuses, and discrepancies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criticism_of_the_Catholic_Church)___ .  [b] The Reformation began in the ___E:Holy Roman Empire U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire)___ [c] in 1517, when ___E:Martin Luther U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther)___ published his Ninety-five Theses as a reaction against abuses in the sale of ___E:indulgences U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indulgence)___ by the Catholic Church, which purported to offer the remission of the ___E:temporal punishment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purgatory)___ of sins to their purchasers.

Luther's statements questioned the Catholic Church's role as negotiator between people and God, especially when it came to the indulgence arrangement, which in part granted people the power to purchase a certificate of pardon for the penalization of their sins. Luther argued against the practice of buying or earning forgiveness, claiming instead that salvation is a gift God gives to those who have faith.

___E:Lutheranism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutheranism)___ spread from Germany [d] into ___E:Denmark–Norway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark%E2%80%93Norway)___ , ___E:Sweden U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Sweden_(1523%E2%80%931611))___ , ___E:Finland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finland_under_Swedish_rule)___ , ___E:Livonia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terra_Mariana)___ , and ___E:Iceland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Iceland#Iceland_under_Norwegian_and_Danish_kings_(1262–1944))___ .  ___E:Calvinist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvinist)___ churches spread in Germany, [e] ___E:Hungary U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hungary_(1526%E2%80%931867))___ , the ___E:Netherlands U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habsburg_Netherlands)___ , ___E:Scotland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Scotland)___ , ___E:Switzerland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Swiss_Confederacy)___ , ___E:France U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_in_the_early_modern_period)___ , ___E:Poland U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_of_the_Kingdom_of_Poland)___ and ___E:Lithuania U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Duchy_of_Lithuania)___ , led by ___E:Protestant Reformers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant_Reformers)___ such as ___E:John Calvin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Calvin)___ , ___E:Huldrych Zwingli U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huldrych_Zwingli)___ and ___E:John Knox U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Knox)___ .

The political separation of the ___E:Church of England U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England)___ from the Catholic Church under ___E:King Henry VIII U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VIII)___ began ___E:Anglicanism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglicanism)___ , bringing England and Wales into this broad Reformation movement, under the leadership of reformer ___E:Thomas Cranmer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Cranmer)___ , whose work forged Anglican doctrine and identity. [f]

Protestantism is divided into various denominations on the basis of ___E:theology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_theology)___ and ___E:ecclesiology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant_ecclesiology)___ .

Protestants adhere to the concept of an ___E:invisible church U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_invisible)___ , in contrast to the Catholic, the Eastern Orthodox Church, the Oriental Orthodox Churches, the ___E:Assyrian Church of the East U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assyrian_Church_of_the_East)___ , and the ___E:Ancient Church of the East U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Church_of_the_East)___ , which all understand themselves as the only original church—the " ___E:one true church U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_true_church)___ "—founded by ___E:Jesus Christ U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus_in_Christianity)___ (though certain Protestant denominations, including historic Lutheranism, hold to this position).

A majority of Protestants [g] are members of a handful of Protestant denominational families; ___E:Adventists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adventism)___ , ___E:Anabaptists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anabaptism)___ , ___E:Anglicans/Episcopalians U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglicanism)___ , ___E:Baptists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baptists)___ , ___E:Calvinist/Reformed U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_Christianity)___ , [h] ___E:Lutherans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutheranism)___ , ___E:Methodists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodism)___ , ___E:Moravians U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moravian_Church)___ , ___E:Pentecostals U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentecostals)___ , ___E:Plymouth Brethren U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plymouth_Brethren)___ , ___E:Presbyterians U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism)___ , ___E:Quakers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakerism)___ and ___E:Waldensians U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waldensians)___ .  ___E:Nondenominational U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nondenominational_Christianity)___ , ___E:charismatic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charismatic_movement)___ and ___E:independent U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_(religion))___ churches are also on the rise, having recently expanded rapidly throughout much of the world, and constitute a significant part of Protestantism.

These various movements, collectively labeled "popular Protestantism" [i] by scholars such as ___E:Peter L. Berger U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_L._Berger)___ , have been called one of the contemporary world's most dynamic religious movements.

___E:Evangelicals U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelicalism)___ , ___E:Pentecostals U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentecostalism)___ , ___E:Independent churches and unaffiliated U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-denominational_Christianity)___ ___E:Christians U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christians)___ are also considered Protestants.     ___E:Hans Hillerbrand U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hans_Hillerbrand&action=edit&redlink=1)___ estimated a total 2004 Protestant population of 833,457,000,  while a report by ___E:Gordon-Conwell Theological Seminary U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordon-Conwell_Theological_Seminary)___ estimated 628,862,000 Protestants in early 2025.  .mw-parser-output .toclimit-2 .toclevel-1 ul,.mw-parser-output .toclimit-3 .toclevel-2 ul,.mw-parser-output .toclimit-4 .toclevel-3 ul,.mw-parser-output .toclimit-5 .toclevel-4 ul,.mw-parser-output .toclimit-6 .toclevel-5 ul,.mw-parser-output .toclimit-7 .toclevel-6 ul{display:none}

Six princes of the ___E:Holy Roman Empire U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire)___ and rulers of fourteen ___E:Imperial Free Cities U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_Free_City)___ , who issued ___E:a protest U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestation_at_Speyer)___ (or dissent) against the edict of the ___E:Diet of Speyer (1529) U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diet_of_Speyer_(1529))___ , were the first individuals to be called Protestants.
The term protestant , though initially purely political in nature, later acquired a broader sense, referring to a member of any Western church which subscribed to the main Protestant principles.
A Protestant is an adherent of any of those Christian bodies that separated from the Church of Rome during the Reformation, or of any group descended from them.
During the Reformation, the term protestant was hardly used outside of German politics.
People who were involved in the religious movement used the word evangelical ( ___E:German U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language)___ : evangelisch ).

Gradually, protestant became a general term, meaning any adherent of the Reformation in the German-speaking area. It was ultimately somewhat taken up by Lutherans, even though ___E:Martin Luther U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther)___ himself insisted on Christian or evangelical as the only acceptable names for individuals who professed faith in Christ. ___E:French U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huguenots)___ and ___E:Swiss Protestants U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformation_in_Switzerland)___ instead preferred the word reformed , which became a popular, neutral, and alternative name for Calvinists.

The word evangelical , which refers to ___E:the gospel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_gospel)___ , was widely used for those involved in the religious movement in the German-speaking area beginning in 1517.  Evangelical is still preferred among some of the historical Protestant denominations in the Lutheran, Calvinist, and United (Lutheran and Reformed) Protestant traditions in Europe, and those with strong ties to them. Above all the term is used by Protestant bodies in the ___E:German-speaking area U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German-speaking_Europe)___ , such as the ___E:Protestant Church in Germany U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant_Church_in_Germany)___ .

Thus, the ___E:German U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language)___ word evangelisch means Protestant, while the German evangelikal , refers to churches shaped by ___E:Evangelicalism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelicalism)___ .

The English word evangelical usually refers to ___E:evangelical Protestant U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelical_Protestant)___ churches, and therefore to a certain part of Protestantism rather than to Protestantism as a whole.

The English word traces its roots back to the ___E:Puritans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puritans)___ in England, where Evangelicalism originated, and then was brought to the ___E:United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States)___ .

Martin Luther always disliked the term Lutheran , preferring the term evangelical , which was derived from euangelion , a Greek word meaning "good news", i.e. " ___E:gospel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gospel)___ ".

The followers of ___E:John Calvin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Calvin)___ , ___E:Huldrych Zwingli U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huldrych_Zwingli)___ , and other theologians linked to the ___E:Reformed tradition U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_tradition)___ also began to use that term. To distinguish the two evangelical groups, others began to refer to the two groups as Evangelical Lutheran and Evangelical Reformed .

Lutherans themselves began to use the term Lutheran in the middle of the 16th century, in order to distinguish themselves from other groups such as the ___E:Philippists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippists)___ and ___E:Calvinists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvinists)___ .

The ___E:German U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language)___ word reformatorisch , which roughly translates to English as "reformational" or "reforming", is used as an alternative for evangelisch in German, and is different from English reformed ( ___E:German U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language)___ : reformiert ), which refers to churches shaped by ideas of ___E:John Calvin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Calvin)___ , ___E:Huldrych Zwingli U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huldrych_Zwingli)___ , and other Reformed theologians.
Derived from the word "Reformation", the term emerged around the same time as Evangelical (1517) and Protestant (1529).
Many experts have proposed criteria to determine whether a Christian denomination should be considered part of Protestantism.
A common consensus approved by most of them is that if a Christian denomination is to be considered Protestant, it must acknowledge the following three fundamental principles of Protestantism.
The belief, emphasized by Luther, in the Bible as the highest source of authority for the church.

The early churches of the Reformation believed in a critical, yet serious, reading of scripture and holding the Bible as a source of authority higher than that of ___E:tradition U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacred_Tradition)___ , though Lutherans cherish tradition for its role in maintaining order and transmitting the Gospel.
The many abuses that had occurred in the Western Church before the Protestant Reformation led the Reformers to reject certain Roman Catholic traditions.

In the early 20th century, a less critical reading of the Bible developed in the United States—leading to a " ___E:fundamentalist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_fundamentalism)___ " reading of Scripture.

Christian fundamentalists read the Bible as the "inerrant, ___E:infallible U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblical_infallibility)___ " Word of God, as do the Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Lutheran and Anglican churches, but interpret it in a ___E:literalist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblical_literalism)___ fashion without using the ___E:historical-critical method U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical-critical_method)___ .

Methodists and Anglicans differ from Lutherans and the Reformed on this doctrine as they teach prima scriptura , which holds that Scripture is the primary source for Christian doctrine, but that "tradition, experience, and reason" can nurture the Christian religion as long as they are in harmony with the Bible ( ___E:Protestant canon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant_Bible)___ ).

___E:Quakers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakers)___ and ___E:Methodists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodist)___ (inclusive of the ___E:holiness movement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holiness_movement)___ ), as well as ___E:Radical Pietists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radical_Pietism)___ , ___E:Pentecostals U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentecostal)___ and ___E:Spiritual Christians U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Christianity)___ emphasize the ___E:Holy Spirit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Spirit_in_Christianity)___ and personal closeness to God.

There was also a time when scripture became the new religious imagery. ___E:Reformed (Calvinist) theology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_Christianity)___ drew out iconoclastic events when John Calvin arrived in Geneva in 1536. Calvin inherited a city where the old medieval Christian world, with its rituals, images, and pilgrims were taken apart.
After the events of the iconoclast in 1566, scripture began to take place of the religious images that were previously removed.

These new text images turned scripture into a visual tool. The absence of traditional images created room for the joint idea of scripture with visual objects, generating a new imagery culture that focused on reading, understanding, and reflecting over observations.

The belief that believers are ___E:justified U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justification_(theology))___ , or pardoned for sin, solely through faith in ___E:Christ U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus)___ rather than a combination of faith and ___E:good works U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_works)___ .
For Protestants, good works are a necessary consequence rather than cause of justification.
However, while justification is by faith alone, there is the position that faith is not nuda fides .

John Calvin explained that "it is therefore faith alone which justifies, and yet the faith which justifies is not alone: just as it is the heat alone of the sun which warms the earth, and yet in the sun it is not alone."  At the time of the justification of an individual, the Lutheran Churches teach that the process of ___E:sanctification U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanctification_in_Christianity)___ commences, which is defined as "the Holy Spirit’s work which follows justification through faith and consists of renewing the believer and bringing forth in him works of renewal."  These ___E:good works U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_works)___ done by Christians are rewarded by God.  Lutheran and Reformed Christians differ from Methodists in their view of the possibility of entire sanctification, with Methodists affirming it as a ___E:second work of grace U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_work_of_grace)___ .

The universal ___E:priesthood of believers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priesthood_of_all_believers)___ implies the right and duty of the Christian laity not only to read the Bible in the ___E:vernacular U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernacular)___ , but also to take part in the government and all the public affairs of the Church.

It is opposed to the hierarchical system which puts the essence and authority of the Church in an exclusive priesthood, and which makes ordained priests the necessary mediators between God and the people.

It is distinguished from the concept of the priesthood of all believers, which did not grant individuals the right to interpret the Bible apart from the Christian community at large because universal priesthood opened the door to such a possibility.
There are scholars who cite that this doctrine tends to subsume all distinctions in the church under a single spiritual entity.

Calvin referred to the universal priesthood as an expression of the relation between the believer and his God, including the freedom of a Christian to come to God through Christ without human mediation.
He also maintained that this principle recognizes Christ as ___E:prophet U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophet)___ , priest, and king and that his priesthood is shared with his people.

Protestants who adhere to the ___E:Nicene Creed U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicene_Creed)___ believe in three ___E:persons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypostasis_(philosophy_and_religion))___ ( ___E:God the Father U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God_the_Father)___ , ___E:God the Son U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God_the_Son)___ , and the ___E:God the Holy Spirit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Spirit_in_Christianity)___ ) as one God.

Movements that emerged around the time of the Protestant Reformation, but are not a part of Protestantism (e.g. ___E:Unitarianism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitarianism)___ ), reject the ___E:Trinity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity)___ .

This often serves as a reason for exclusion of the ___E:Unitarian Universalism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitarian_Universalism)___ , ___E:Oneness Pentecostalism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oneness_Pentecostalism)___ , and other movements from Protestantism by various observers.
Unitarianism continues to have a presence mainly in ___E:Transylvania U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transylvania)___ , England, and the United States.

The Five solae are five ___E:Latin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin)___ phrases (or slogans) that emerged during the ___E:Protestant Reformation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant_Reformation)___ and summarize the reformers' basic differences in theological beliefs in opposition to the teaching of the ___E:Catholic Church U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church)___ of the day.  The Latin word sola means "alone", "only", or "single".
The use of the phrases as summaries of teaching emerged over time during the Reformation, based on the overarching Lutheran and Reformed principle of sola scriptura (by scripture alone).

This idea contains the four main doctrines on the Bible: that its teaching is needed for salvation (necessity); that all the doctrine necessary for salvation comes from the Bible alone (sufficiency); that everything taught in the Bible is correct (inerrancy); and that, by the Holy Spirit overcoming sin, believers may read and understand truth from the Bible itself, though understanding is difficult, so the means used to guide individual believers to the true teaching is often mutual discussion within the church (clarity).

The necessity and inerrancy were well-established ideas, garnering little criticism, though they later came under debate from outside during the ___E:Enlightenment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment)___ .
The most contentious idea at the time though was the notion that anyone could simply pick up the Bible and learn enough to gain salvation.
The second main principle, sola fide (by faith alone), states that faith in Christ is sufficient alone for eternal salvation and justification.
Though argued from scripture, and hence logically consequent to sola scriptura , this is the guiding principle of the work of Luther and the later reformers.

Because sola scriptura placed the Bible as the only source of teaching, sola fide epitomizes the main thrust of the teaching the reformers wanted to get back to, namely the direct, close, personal connection between Christ and the believer, hence the reformers' contention that their work was Christocentric.
The other solas, as statements, emerged later, but the thinking they represent was also part of the early Reformation.
The Protestant movement began to diverge into several distinct branches in the mid-to-late 16th century.
One of the central points of divergence was controversy over the ___E:Eucharist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eucharist)___ .

Early Protestants rejected the Catholic ___E:dogma U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dogma)___ of ___E:transubstantiation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transubstantiation)___ , which teaches that the bread and wine used in the sacrificial rite of the Mass lose their natural substance by being transformed into the body, blood, soul, and divinity of Christ.
They disagreed with one another concerning the presence of Christ and his body and blood in Holy Communion.

Protestants reject the Catholic doctrine of ___E:papal supremacy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papal_supremacy)___ , and have variant views on the number of ___E:sacraments U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacrament)___ , the ___E:real presence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_presence_of_Christ_in_the_Eucharist)___ of ___E:Christ U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus_in_Christianity)___ in the ___E:Eucharist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eucharist)___ , and matters of ___E:ecclesiastical polity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecclesiastical_polity)___ and ___E:apostolic succession U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apostolic_succession)___ .

Many of the individual ideas that were taken up by various reformers had historical pre-cursors; however, calling them proto-reformers is controversial, as often their theology also had components that are not associated with later Protestants, or that were asserted by some Protestants but denied by others, or that were only superficially similar.

One of the earliest persons to be praised as a Protestant forerunner is ___E:Jovinian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jovinian)___ , who lived in the fourth century AD. He attacked ___E:monasticism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monasticism)___ , ___E:ascetism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asceticism)___ and believed that a saved believer can never be overcome by Satan.
In the 9th century, the theologian ___E:Gottschalk of Orbais U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gottschalk_of_Orbais)___ was condemned for heresy by the Catholic Church.
Gottschalk believed that the salvation of Jesus was limited and that his redemption was only for the elect.

The theology of Gottschalk anticipated the Protestant reformation.   [self-published source?] ___E:Ratramnus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ratramnus)___ also defended the theology of Gottschalk and denied the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist; his writings also influenced the later Protestant reformation.  ___E:Claudius of Turin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudius_of_Turin)___ in the 9th century also held Protestant ideas, such as ___E:faith alone U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sola_fide)___ and rejection of the supremacy of Peter.

In the late 1130s, ___E:Arnold of Brescia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_of_Brescia)___ , an Italian ___E:canon regular U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canon_regular)___ became one of the first theologians to attempt to reform the Catholic Church.

After his death, his teachings on ___E:apostolic poverty U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apostolic_poverty)___ gained currency among ___E:Arnoldists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnoldists)___ , and later more widely among ___E:Waldensians U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waldensians)___ and the ___E:Spiritual Franciscans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Franciscans)___ , though no written word of his has survived the official condemnation.
In the early 1170s, ___E:Peter Waldo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Waldo)___ founded the Waldensians.
He advocated an interpretation of the Gospel that led to conflicts with the Catholic Church.
By 1215, the Waldensians were declared heretical and subject to persecution.
Despite that, the movement continues to exist to this day in Italy, as ___E:a part of the wider Reformed tradition U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waldensian_Evangelical_Church)___ .

In the 1370s, Oxford theologian and priest ___E:John Wycliffe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wycliffe)___ —later dubbed the "Morning Star of Reformation"—started his activity as an English reformer.

He rejected papal authority over secular power (in that any person in mortal sin lost their authority and should be resisted: a priest with possessions, such as a pope, was in such grave sin), may have ___E:translated the Bible U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wycliffe%27s_Bible)___ into ___E:vernacular U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernacular)___ English, and preached anticlerical and biblically centred reforms.
His rejection of a real divine presence in the elements of the Eucharist foreshadowed Huldrych Zwingli's similar ideas in the 16th century.
Wycliffe's admirers came to be known as " ___E:Lollards U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lollardy)___ ".

Beginning in the first decade of the 15th century, ___E:Jan Hus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Hus)___ —a Catholic priest, Czech reformist and professor—influenced by John Wycliffe's writings, founded the ___E:Hussite U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hussite)___ movement.
He strongly advocated his reformist ___E:Bohemian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohemia)___ religious denomination.

He was ___E:excommunicated U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excommunication)___ and ___E:burned at the stake U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burned_at_the_stake)___ in ___E:Constance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konstanz)___ , ___E:Bishopric of Constance U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishopric_of_Constance)___ , in 1415 by secular authorities for unrepentant and persistent heresy.
After his execution, a revolt erupted.
Hussites defeated five continuous crusades proclaimed against them by the ___E:Pope U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope)___ .

Later theological disputes caused a split within the Hussite movement. ___E:Utraquists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utraquism)___ maintained that both the bread and the wine should be administered to the people during the Eucharist.

Another major faction were the ___E:Taborites U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taborites)___ , who opposed the Utraquists in the ___E:Battle of Lipany U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lipany)___ during the ___E:Hussite Wars U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hussite_Wars)___ .
There were two separate parties among the Hussites: moderate and radical movements.

Other smaller regional Hussite branches in ___E:Bohemia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohemia)___ included ___E:Adamites U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adamites)___ , ___E:Orebites U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orebites)___ , ___E:Orphans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sirotci)___ , and Praguers.

The Great Awakenings were periods of rapid and dramatic religious revival in Anglo-American religious history.

The ___E:First Great Awakening U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Great_Awakening)___ was an evangelical and revitalization movement that swept through Protestant Europe and ___E:British America U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_America)___ , especially the ___E:American colonies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirteen_Colonies)___ in the 1730s and 1740s, leaving a permanent impact on ___E:American Protestantism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestantism_in_the_United_States)___ .
It resulted from powerful preaching that gave listeners a sense of deep personal revelation of their need of salvation by Jesus Christ.

Pulling away from ritual, ceremony, sacramentalism and hierarchy, it made Christianity intensely personal to the average person by fostering a deep sense of spiritual conviction and redemption, and by encouraging introspection and a commitment to a new standard of personal morality.

The ___E:Second Great Awakening U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Great_Awakening)___ began around 1790. It gained momentum by 1800. After 1820, membership rose rapidly among ___E:Baptist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baptist)___ and ___E:Methodist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodism)___ congregations, whose preachers led the movement.
It was past its peak by the late 1840s.

It has been described as a reaction against skepticism, ___E:deism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deism)___ , and ___E:rationalism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rationalism)___ , although why those forces became pressing enough at the time to spark revivals is not fully understood.
It enrolled millions of new members in existing ___E:evangelical U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelical)___ denominations and led to the formation of new denominations.

The ___E:Third Great Awakening U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Great_Awakening)___ refers to a hypothetical historical period that was marked by religious activism in ___E:American history U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_history)___ and spans the late 1850s to the early 20th century.
It affected ___E:pietistic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pietistic)___ Protestant denominations and had a strong element of social activism.

It was affiliated with the ___E:Social Gospel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Gospel)___ Movement, which applied Christianity to social issues and gained its force from the Awakening, as did the worldwide missionary movement.

New groupings emerged, such as the ___E:Holiness U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holiness_movement)___ , ___E:Nazarene U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_the_Nazarene)___ , and ___E:Christian Science U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Science)___ movements.

The ___E:Fourth Great Awakening U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Great_Awakening)___ was a Christian religious awakening that some scholars—most notably, ___E:Robert Fogel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Fogel)___ —say took place in the United States in the late 1960s and early 1970s, while others look at the era following ___E:World War II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II)___ .

A noteworthy development in 20th-century Protestant Christianity was the rise of the modern ___E:Pentecostal movement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentecostalism)___ .

Sprung from Methodist and ___E:Wesleyan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wesley)___ roots, it arose out of meetings at an urban mission on ___E:Azusa Street U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azusa_Street)___ in Los Angeles.

In Europe, there has been a general move away from religious observance and belief in Christian teachings and a move towards ___E:secularism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secularism)___ .
The ___E:Enlightenment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment)___ is largely responsible for the spread of secularism.

However, the sole example of France demonstrates that even in Catholic-majority countries, the overwhelming impact of the Enlightenment has brought even stronger secularism and freedom of thought five centuries later.
It is more reliable to consider that the Reformation influenced the critical thinkers of the subsequent centuries.

Initial philosophers of the Enlightenment were defending a Christian conception of the world, but it was developed together with a fierce and decisive criticism of the Church, its politics, its ethics, its worldview, its scientific and cultural assumptions, leading to the devaluation of all forms of institutionalized Christianity, which extended over the centuries.

The Radical Reformation was non-mainstream, though in parts of Germany, Switzerland and Austria, a majority would sympathize with the Radical Reformation despite the intense persecution it faced from both Catholics and Magisterial Protestants.

The early ___E:Anabaptists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anabaptists)___ believed that their reformation must purify not only theology but also the actual lives of Christians, especially their political and social relationships.

This was not a doctrine new to the reformers, but was taught by earlier groups, such as the ___E:Albigenses U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catharism)___ in 1147. Though most of the Radical Reformers were Anabaptist, some did not identify themselves with the mainstream Anabaptist tradition. ___E:Thomas Müntzer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_M%C3%BCntzer)___ was involved in the ___E:German Peasants' War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Peasants%27_War)___ . ___E:Andreas Karlstadt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreas_Karlstadt)___ disagreed theologically with Huldrych Zwingli and Martin Luther, teaching nonviolence and refusing to baptize infants while not rebaptizing adult believers.  ___E:Kaspar Schwenkfeld U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaspar_Schwenkfeld)___ and ___E:Sebastian Franck U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sebastian_Franck)___ were influenced by ___E:German mysticism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_mysticism)___ and ___E:spiritualism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritualism_(movement))___ .
In the view of many associated with the Radical Reformation, the ___E:Magisterial Reformation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magisterial_Reformation)___ had not gone far enough.

Radical Reformer, ___E:Andreas von Bodenstein Karlstadt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreas_Karlstadt)___ , for example, referred to the Lutheran theologians at ___E:Wittenberg U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wittenberg)___ as the "new papists".
Since the term "magister" also means "teacher", the Magisterial Reformation is also characterized by an emphasis on the authority of a teacher.
This is made evident in the prominence of Luther, Calvin, and Zwingli as leaders of the reform movements in their respective areas of ministry.
Because of their authority, they were often criticized by Radical Reformers as being too much like the Roman Popes.

A more political side of the Radical Reformation can be seen in the thought and practice of ___E:Hans Hut U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Hut)___ , although typically Anabaptism has been associated with pacifism.

Anabaptism in shape of its various diversification such as the ___E:Amish U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amish)___ , ___E:Mennonites U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mennonites)___ and ___E:Hutterites U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hutterites)___ came out of the Radical Reformation.

Later in history, ___E:Schwarzenau Brethren U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwarzenau_Brethren)___ , and the ___E:Apostolic Christian Church U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apostolic_Christian_Church)___ would emerge in Anabaptist circles.

Protestants refer to specific groupings of congregations or churches that share in common foundational doctrines and the name of their groups as ___E:denominations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Christian_Denominations#Protestant)___ .
The term denomination (national body) is to be distinguished from branch (denominational family; tradition), communion (international body) and congregation (church).

Protestants reject the ___E:Catholic Church U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church)___ 's doctrine that it is the ___E:one true church U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_true_church)___ , with some teaching belief in the invisible church , which consists of all who profess faith in Jesus Christ.

The ___E:Lutheran Church U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutheranism)___ traditionally sees itself as the "main trunk of the historical Christian Tree" founded by Christ and the Apostles, holding that during the Reformation, the ___E:Church of Rome U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_See)___ fell away. Other denominations are simply regional or ethnic expressions of the same beliefs.

Because the five solas are the main tenets of the Protestant faith, ___E:non-denominational U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nondenominational_Christianity)___ groups and organizations are also considered Protestant.

Most denominations share common beliefs in the major aspects of the Christian faith while differing in many secondary doctrines, although what is major and what is secondary is a matter of idiosyncratic belief.

United and uniting churches are churches formed from the merger or other form of union of two or more different Protestant denominations.
Historically, unions of Protestant churches were enforced by the state, usually in order to have a stricter control over the religious sphere of its people, but also for other organizational reasons.

As modern ___E:Christian ecumenism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_ecumenism)___ progresses, unions between various Protestant traditions are becoming more and more common, resulting in a growing number of united and uniting churches.

Some of the recent major examples are the ___E:Church of North India U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_North_India)___ (1970), ___E:United Protestant Church of France U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Protestant_Church_of_France)___ (2013), and the ___E:Protestant Church in the Netherlands U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant_Church_in_the_Netherlands)___ (2004).

As mainline Protestantism shrinks in ___E:Europe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe)___ and ___E:North America U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America)___ due to the rise of ___E:secularism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secularism)___ or in areas where Christianity is a minority religion as with the ___E:Indian subcontinent U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_subcontinent)___ , ___E:Reformed U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_church)___ , ___E:Anglican U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican)___ , and ___E:Lutheran U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutheran)___ denominations merge, often creating large nationwide denominations.

What is perhaps the oldest official united church is found in ___E:Germany U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany)___ , where the ___E:Protestant Church in Germany U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant_Church_in_Germany)___ is a federation of ___E:Lutheran U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutheranism)___ , United ( ___E:Prussian Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prussian_Union_of_churches)___ ), and ___E:Reformed churches U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_churches)___ , dating back to 1817.
Around the world, each united or uniting church comprises a different mix of predecessor Protestant denominations.

Trends are visible, however, as most united and uniting churches have one or more predecessors with heritage in the ___E:Reformed tradition U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvinism)___ and many are members of the ___E:World Alliance of Reformed Churches U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Alliance_of_Reformed_Churches)___ .
Protestants can be differentiated according to how they have been influenced by important movements since the Reformation, today regarded as branches.
Some of these movements have a common lineage, sometimes directly spawning individual denominations.

___E:Lutheranism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutheranism)___ identifies with the ___E:theology of Martin Luther U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theology_of_Martin_Luther)___ .

It advocates a doctrine of justification "by ___E:grace alone U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sola_gratia)___ through ___E:faith alone U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sola_fide)___ on the basis of ___E:Scripture alone U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sola_scriptura)___ ", the doctrine that scripture is the final authority on all matters of faith, rejecting the assertion made by Catholic leaders at the ___E:Council of Trent U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Trent)___ that authority comes from both Scriptures and ___E:Tradition U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacred_tradition)___ .
In addition, Lutherans accept the teachings of the first four ___E:ecumenical councils U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecumenical_councils)___ of the undivided Christian Church.

Unlike the Reformed tradition, Lutherans retain many of the ___E:liturgical U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_liturgy)___ practices and ___E:sacramental U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacraments#Lutheran_teaching)___ teachings of the pre-Reformation Church with an emphasis on the ___E:Eucharist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramental_union)___ , or Lord's Supper.

Today, Lutheranism is one of the largest branches of Protestantism.

With approximately 80 million adherents,  it constitutes the third most common Protestant confession after historically ___E:Pentecostal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentecostal)___ denominations and ___E:Anglicanism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglicanism)___ .
The ___E:Lutheran World Federation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutheran_World_Federation)___ , the largest global communion of Lutheran churches represents over 72 million people.

___E:Anglicanism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglicanism)___ consists of the ___E:Church of England U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England)___ and churches which are historically tied to it or hold similar beliefs, worship practices and church structures.
The word Anglican originates in ecclesia anglicana , a ___E:medieval Latin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_Latin)___ phrase dating to at least 1246 that means the English Church .
There is no single "Anglican Church" with universal juridical authority, since each national or regional church has full ___E:autonomy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autonomy)___ .

As the name suggests, the communion is an association of churches in ___E:full communion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full_communion)___ with the ___E:archbishop of Canterbury U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archbishop_of_Canterbury)___ .

The great majority of Anglicans are members of churches which are part of the international ___E:Anglican Communion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Communion)___ ,  which has 85 million adherents.

The ___E:Church of England U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England)___ declared its independence from the Catholic Church at the time of the ___E:Elizabethan Religious Settlement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabethan_Religious_Settlement)___ .
Many of the new Anglican formularies of the mid-16th century corresponded closely to those of contemporary Reformed tradition.

These reforms were understood by one of those most responsible for them, the then archbishop of Canterbury, ___E:Thomas Cranmer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Cranmer)___ , as navigating a middle way between two of the emerging Protestant traditions, namely Lutheranism and Calvinism.
Unique to Anglicanism is the Book of Common Prayer , the collection of services that worshippers in most Anglican churches used for centuries.

While it has since undergone many revisions and Anglican churches in different countries have developed other service books, the Book of Common Prayer is still acknowledged as one of the ties that bind the Anglican Communion together.

The ___E:Thirty-Nine Articles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirty-Nine_Articles)___ and the ___E:Books of Homilies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Books_of_Homilies)___ explicate historic Anglican doctrine and along with the Book of Common Prayer, were developed under the reformer Thomas Cranmer.

___E:Calvinism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvinism)___ , also called the Reformed tradition, was advanced by several theologians such as ___E:Martin Bucer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Bucer)___ , ___E:Heinrich Bullinger U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_Bullinger)___ , ___E:Peter Martyr Vermigli U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Martyr_Vermigli)___ , and Huldrych Zwingli, but this branch of Christianity bears the name of the French reformer John Calvin because of his prominent influence on it and because of his role in the confessional and ecclesiastical debates throughout the 16th century.
This term also refers to the doctrines and practices of the ___E:Reformed churches U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_churches)___ of which Calvin was an early leader.
Less commonly, it can refer to the individual teaching of Calvin himself.

The particulars of Calvinist theology may be stated in a number of ways. Perhaps the best known summary is contained in the ___E:five points of Calvinism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_points_of_Calvinism)___ , though these points identify the Calvinist view on ___E:soteriology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_soteriology)___ rather than summarizing the system as a whole.

Broadly speaking, Calvinism stresses the sovereignty or rule of God in all things—in salvation but also in all of life. This concept is seen clearly in the doctrines of ___E:predestination U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Predestination_(Calvinism))___ and ___E:total depravity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_depravity)___ .

___E:Methodism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodism)___ identifies principally with ___E:the theology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wesleyan_theology)___ of ___E:John Wesley U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wesley)___ .

___E:Soteriologically U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soteriology)___ , most Methodists are ___E:Arminian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arminian)___ , emphasizing that Christ accomplished salvation for every human being, and that humans must exercise an act of the will to receive it (as opposed to the traditional Calvinist doctrine of ___E:monergism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monergism)___ ).

The ___E:Free Methodist Church U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Methodist_Church)___ , the ___E:Salvation Army U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvation_Army)___ and the ___E:Wesleyan Methodist Church U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wesleyan_Church)___ are notable examples, while other adherents of the Holiness Movement remained within mainline Methodism, e.g. the ___E:United Methodist Church U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Methodist_Church)___ .

___E:Pentecostalism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentecostalism)___ is a movement that places special emphasis on a direct personal experience of ___E:God U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God_in_Christianity)___ through the ___E:baptism with the Holy Spirit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baptism_with_the_Holy_Spirit)___ .

Contrary to how the Protestant Reformers were often characterized, the concept of a catholic or universal Church was not brushed aside during the Protestant Reformation.
On the contrary, the visible unity of the catholic or universal church was seen by the Protestant reformers as an important and essential doctrine of the Reformation.

The Magisterial reformers, such as Martin Luther, John Calvin, and Huldrych Zwingli, believed that they were reforming the Catholic Church, which they viewed as having become corrupted. [p] Each of them took very seriously the charges of schism and innovation, denying these charges and maintaining that it was the Catholic Church that had left them. The Protestant Reformers formed a new and radically different theological opinion on ecclesiology, that the visible Church is "catholic" (lower-case "c") rather than "Catholic" (upper-case "C").

Accordingly, there is not an indefinite number of parochial, congregational or national churches, constituting, as it were, so many ecclesiastical individualities, but one great spiritual republic of which these various organizations form a part, [q] although they each have very different opinions.
This was markedly far-removed from the traditional and historic Catholic understanding that the Catholic Church was the one true Church of Christ. [r]

Yet, in the Protestant understanding, the visible church is not a genus, so to speak, with so many species under it. [s] In order to justify their departure [t] from the Catholic Church, Protestants often posited a new argument, [u] saying that there was no real visible Church with divine authority, only a spiritual, invisible, and hidden church —this notion began in the early days of the Protestant Reformation.

Wherever the Magisterial Reformation, which received support from the ruling authorities, took place, the result was a reformed national Protestant church envisioned to be a part of the whole invisible church , but disagreeing, in certain important points of doctrine and doctrine-linked practice, with what had until then been considered the normative reference point on such matters, [v] namely the Papacy and central authority of the Catholic Church.

The Reformed churches thus believed in some form of Catholicity, founded on their doctrines of the five solas and a visible ___E:ecclesiastical U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecclesiastical)___ organization based on the 14th- and 15th-century ___E:Conciliar movement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conciliarism)___ , rejecting the ___E:papacy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papacy)___ and ___E:papal infallibility U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papal_infallibility)___ in favor of ___E:ecumenical councils U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecumenical_council)___ , but rejecting the latest ecumenical council, the ___E:Council of Trent U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Trent)___ . [w] Religious unity therefore became not one of doctrine and identity but one of invisible character, wherein the unity was one of faith in Jesus Christ, not common identity, doctrine, belief, and collaborative action.
